terms.plain: A demand from a fund for investors to send in some of the money they committed. Private funds draw capital down as deals happen rather than taking it all up front.
terms.formal: A notice requiring limited partners to transfer a portion of their committed capital, typically to fund an investment or expenses, within a short specified period.

terms.plain: The manager's share of the profits, usually around 20%, paid only above a minimum return. It is the main way private fund managers get paid.
terms.formal: The general partner's share of fund profits, typically 20% above a preferred return, distributed according to the fund's waterfall provisions.

terms.plain: The total amount you promise to a private fund. Only part of it is called at any time, so the money must stay available for years.
terms.formal: The aggregate capital an investor contractually agrees to provide to a fund over its investment period, drawn down through capital calls rather than funded at closing.

terms.plain: Cash actually returned divided by cash actually called. The one private markets figure that cannot be argued with, because it is realised money.
terms.formal: Cumulative distributions divided by paid-in capital, measuring realised return without reliance on unrealised valuations.

terms.plain: Committed capital a fund has not yet called or invested. High industry dry powder means more competition for deals and usually higher entry prices.
terms.formal: Undrawn committed capital available for investment, whose aggregate level across a strategy is an indicator of competitive pressure on entry valuations.

terms.plain: A limit on how much can be redeemed from a fund in one period. It protects remaining investors from a rush for the exit, and traps you if you wanted out.
terms.formal: A provision capping aggregate or per-investor redemptions in a given period, designed to prevent forced liquidation of illiquid assets at the expense of remaining holders.

terms.plain: The shape a private fund's returns trace over its life: negative early on, because fees are charged and investments have not matured, then rising as investments are sold. Plotted over time it looks like the letter J.
terms.formal: The characteristic trajectory of a closed-end private fund's cumulative net return, initially negative due to fees and unrealised early-stage holdings, then improving as value is realised.

terms.plain: A period during which you cannot get your money out of a fund at all.
terms.formal: A contractual period following investment during which redemption is prohibited, used to match investor liquidity to the underlying strategy's horizon.

terms.plain: Total value divided by money invested. A 2.5x MOIC means you got two and a half times your money back — but it says nothing about how long that took.
terms.formal: The ratio of total realised and unrealised value to invested capital, insensitive to timing and therefore quoted alongside IRR.

terms.plain: What a fund is worth: everything it owns minus everything it owes. Exposures are quoted as a percentage of it, so 130% long means long positions worth 1.3 times the fund's capital.
terms.formal: Total fund assets less total liabilities, the denominator against which exposures, leverage and per-unit values are expressed.

terms.plain: What the fund still holds, at the manager's own valuation, divided by cash called. It is an estimate, not a result.
terms.formal: Unrealised net asset value divided by paid-in capital, representing the portion of reported performance dependent on the manager's valuations.

terms.plain: Buying an existing investor's stake in a private fund, or a portfolio of assets, from them rather than committing to a new fund. Usually at a discount.
terms.formal: Transactions in existing private fund interests or asset portfolios, providing liquidity to sellers and typically transacted at a discount to reported net asset value.

terms.plain: A part of a fund holding assets that cannot be valued or sold normally, carved out so the rest of the fund can still be redeemed.
terms.formal: A segregated portion of a fund containing illiquid or hard-to-value positions, excluded from ordinary redemption and realised separately.

terms.plain: A credit facility a fund uses to pay for deals before calling investor money. It shortens the period investor capital is outstanding, which raises the reported IRR.
terms.formal: A revolving credit facility secured against limited partner commitments, used to defer capital calls and thereby compress the measurement period over which IRR is calculated.

terms.plain: Everything the fund is worth — cash returned plus what it still holds — divided by cash called. Early in a fund's life it is mostly the manager's own opinion.
terms.formal: The sum of distributions and residual value divided by paid-in capital. Equals DPI plus RVPI, and is dominated by unrealised marks in a fund's early years.

terms.plain: The year a private fund started investing. It largely determines the prices it paid and the conditions it exited into, which is why funds are compared within vintages.
terms.formal: The year in which a fund makes its first investment, used as the primary basis for peer comparison because entry pricing, credit availability and exit conditions are cycle-dependent.
